title: A mesh figure answers one question: are the cells the right size, in the right places, with the boundaries labelled?
summary: A structured mesh is a bookkeeping device: it fixes how many unknowns there are, how big each cell is, and where each boundary sits. Reading one means counting cells, checking spacing and boundary labels, and knowing what a coarser or finer version of the same mesh costs and buys.

media.alt: A square unit domain covered by a uniform 64 by 64 grid of square cells, drawn with thin blue and grey lines. The four edges are drawn in red and labelled West, East, North (wall/outlet) and South (wall/inlet). The title states 4096 cells with spacing 0.016 m in both directions.

source.caption: 2D structured mesh, 64x64
source.note: Group: three 2D meshes (16x16, 32x32, 64x64), one 1D mesh of 20 cells, two smoke-test meshes and one smoke-test scalar field. These are set-up and sanity-check figures; none of them shows a flow solution.

read_the_figure.question: Is the grid adequate for the problem: how many cells, how large, how uniform, and where are the boundaries?
read_the_figure.axes: x and y: physical position in metres. The domain is the unit square, 0 to 1 m in both directions. Each small box is one control volume (cell). Red lines are the domain boundary; the title gives the cell count and the spacing.
look_at: The title first: it states the cell count and the spacing (64 x 64 = 4096 cells, spacing 0.016 m). Check that the arithmetic closes: 1 m divided by 64 is 0.0156 m, printed as 0.016.
Are the cells uniform? Equal spacing means the same truncation error everywhere, which is the simplest case for convergence studies. Stretched meshes would show lines bunching near walls.

The red boundary labels (West, East, North, South) tell you where boundary conditions are applied. Here North and South carry extra words (wall/outlet, wall/inlet), so the bottom edge is where flow would enter and the top edge where it would leave.
In the 1D mesh, the blue vertical lines are cell faces and the red dots are cell centres. Centres sit halfway between faces: 20 cells over 1 m give spacing 0.05 m and the first centre at 0.025 m.

The 16x16, 32x32 and 64x64 figures are the same domain at three resolutions. Each step halves the spacing (about 0.0625, 0.031 and 0.0156 m by the same arithmetic) and multiplies the cell count by four.
read_the_figure.proves: Only set-up facts: the domain, the cell count, the spacing and the boundary labels. A mesh figure cannot show that a solution is accurate. What it can prove is that the refinement sequence was constructed consistently (constant ratio of two) so that a later convergence plot is meaningful.
if_wrong: Cell count in the title does not match the lines drawn: the figure was produced from a different mesh than the one used in the run.
Spacing changes between refinements by a ratio other than a constant: observed orders computed from those meshes are not reliable.
Boundaries are unlabelled or labelled inconsistently with the problem statement: a wall may have been treated as an outlet.

The smoke-test scalar field looks like uncorrelated noise from cell to cell: for a smoke test this is expected if the field was filled with random numbers just to check that plotting and indexing work. It must not be read as physics.
must_check: Cell count and spacing printed, and they agree with each other.
Aspect ratio of cells (here 1, square) is stated or visible.
Boundary names present, and each is mapped to a boundary condition elsewhere.
Axes in physical units with equal scaling, so squares look like squares.
For a refinement set: constant ratio between successive meshes.
A field plotted on a mesh states which mesh (here the smoke-test field title says 16x16).
as_drawn: The 64x64 mesh title: 4096 cells, spacing 0.016 m by 0.016 m. Boundary labels: West, East, North (wall / outlet), South (wall / inlet).
The 1D mesh title: 20 cells, spacing about 0.0500 m, domain 0 to 1 m. Cell centres are marked with red dots.

The smoke-test field is titled 'phi on a 16x16 mesh' and ranges between about 0.0 and 1.0 on its colour bar with no visible spatial pattern, consistent with a random fill used to test plotting rather than a solved field. This is an inference from the image, not from the project text.

terms.meaning: A small region of space over which a conservation law is balanced. The unknown stored on it is an average value.
Unknowns are stored at centres in a cell-centred finite-volume scheme. Fluxes are evaluated on the faces between neighbours.
A grid whose cells are indexed by integers (i, j), so neighbours are found by adding or subtracting one. Simple and fast, but only fits simple shapes.
The cell width. For a uniform mesh with N cells over length L it is L divided by N.
The number of unknowns the solver has to find. For one scalar on an N by N mesh it is N squared.
The factor by which spacing shrinks between successive meshes. Verification studies keep it constant, commonly 2.
A deliberately trivial run whose only purpose is to show that the code runs end to end: mesh built, field allocated, plot produced.
The rule that closes the problem on a boundary: a fixed value (Dirichlet), a fixed gradient (Neumann), or a mix.

remember: A mesh is part of the numerical method: change the mesh and you change the answer.
Cell count in d dimensions grows as (1/h)^d. Halving h in 2D multiplies cells by 4, in 3D by 8.
Cell centres sit at x_i = (i + 1/2) h for cell index i = 0 to N - 1.
Explicit time stepping makes cost grow faster than the cell count, because the stable time step also shrinks with h.
A smoke-test figure proves the pipeline works. It never proves the physics is right.

understand.title: Why a mesh at all
understand.text: A computer cannot store a continuous function, only a finite list of numbers. A mesh decides what that list means: one number per cell. Everything the solver later does, differences, fluxes, time steps, is arithmetic on that list.

understand.title: What the three resolutions are for
understand.text: The 16x16, 32x32 and 64x64 meshes are one refinement sequence. Running the same case on all three is the raw material of a grid-convergence study: if the answer changes by less each time and at the expected rate, the discretization error is under control.

understand.title: What the 1D picture adds
understand.text: The 1D mesh draws the objects a 2D picture hides: faces (lines) and centres (dots). It makes clear that values live at centres but fluxes are computed at faces.

steps.title: Spacing from cell count
steps.note: This reproduces the title of the figure: the printed 0.016 is 0.015625 rounded. The 1D mesh gives 1/20 = 0.05 m the same way.

steps.title: Where cell centres sit
steps.note: For the 1D mesh with h = 0.05 m the first centre is at 0.025 m and the last at 0.975 m, which is exactly what the red dots show.

steps.title: Cells grow as a power of the refinement
steps.note: In 2D the three meshes in this group have 256, 1024 and 4096 cells.

steps.title: Cost of an explicit diffusion step
steps.note: Standard stability limit for the explicit scheme. Halving h cuts the allowed time step by four.

steps.title: Work for a fixed end time
steps.note: Each refinement of the 2D mesh multiplies the work of an explicit diffusion run by 2^4 = 16. This is why a mesh is chosen, not simply made as fine as possible.

steps.title: Error and spacing
steps.note: Why three meshes: the ratio of errors on two successive meshes gives the observed order. With a second-order scheme the error should fall by a factor 4 each refinement. See the linked concept page for the full argument.

worked.title: Cells and work when going from 16x16 to 64x64
worked.problem: A diffusion problem is run with an explicit scheme on the 16x16 mesh and then on the 64x64 mesh, both to the same end time. By what factors do the cell count and the number of cell-updates grow?

solution.text: Spacing shrinks by 4 (from 1/16 to 1/64), so the stable explicit time step shrinks by 4 squared.

worked.answer: 16 times more cells and 256 times more cell-updates. The mesh is four times finer in each direction but the run is two orders of magnitude more expensive.

analyze.q: The 64x64 mesh title says spacing 0.016 m but 1/64 is 0.015625. Is the figure wrong? What does it tell you about how to read printed numbers on a mesh figure?
You need to compare solutions on the 16x16, 32x32 and 64x64 meshes. List what must be identical across the three runs besides the domain.
analyze.hint: Boundary conditions, time step or its scaling, solver tolerance, initial condition.

analyze.q: The smoke-test field is visually noise. Which of these claims can the figure support: the code runs, the plotting works, the scheme is accurate?
analyze.hint: Think about what a random field can test.

evaluate.q: For a flow with a thin boundary layer on the South wall, is a uniform 64x64 mesh a good choice? What would you change?
evaluate.hint: Where do the gradients live, and where are the cells?

evaluate.q: Is it enough to show only the 64x64 mesh in a report? What does the reader lose compared with the whole refinement set?
evaluate.hint: A single mesh cannot show a trend.

create: Design a stretched 1D mesh of 20 cells with a constant stretching ratio that is finest at the left wall. State the ratio and the first cell width, and draw it in the same style as the uniform one.
Add the three annotations a mesh figure should always carry (cell count, minimum and maximum spacing, boundary-condition names) to a 2D mesh figure of your own.

checks.q: Why does a finite-volume solver store values at cell centres but compute fluxes at faces?
checks.hint: What does a conservation balance need to know?
checks.answer: The balance for one cell is what flows in minus what flows out through its faces. The flux is an interface quantity, so it is evaluated on the faces from the neighbouring centre values; the cell average at the centre is the unknown being updated.

checks.q: A 3D box is meshed with 32 cells per side and then refined to 64 per side. How many times more cells?
Two runs on the 64x64 mesh give different answers although the mesh is identical. Name two causes that are not the mesh.
checks.hint: Everything else that is part of the set-up.
checks.answer: For example a different time step, a different solver tolerance, different boundary treatment, a different initial condition or a random seed in the set-up. The mesh is only one of the inputs to the answer.

checks.q: A report shows a mesh figure and says 'the mesh is fine enough'. What is missing?
checks.hint: Mesh adequacy is shown by a comparison, not by a picture.
checks.answer: A comparison between at least two or three resolutions showing that the quantity of interest stops changing, or changes at the expected rate. A picture of one mesh shows only what was built.

checks.q: How would you build a three-mesh refinement set for a 1 m channel so that observed order is measurable?
checks.hint: Constant ratio, and the coarsest mesh must already be inside the asymptotic range.
checks.answer: Choose counts that double, for example 20, 40 and 80 cells per metre, keep the same boundary conditions and a time step that is small enough or refined consistently, run the same case on each, and compute the base-2 logarithm of successive error ratios.
